title: India's Commerce Minister Says the US Trade Deal Is '99% Done.' The Last 1% Is the Hard Part.
excerpt: As American negotiators wrap up four days of talks in New Delhi, a new 12.5% tariff threat under Section 301 complicates what was supposed to be a triumphant finish.
body:
A high-level US delegation led by Chief Negotiator Brendan Lynch is wrapping up four days of talks in New Delhi that both sides say have brought the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement to the brink of completion. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal recently described the deal as "99 percent done." But the final stretch is turning out to be the most fraught.

The negotiations, held from June 1 to 4, have covered market access, non-tariff measures, customs and trade facilitation, investment promotion and what the Commerce Ministry calls "economic security alignment" — a relatively new phrase in India-US trade vocabulary that reflects the strategic dimension both countries are now building into commercial ties.

## The Section 301 Shadow

Even as the interim trade pact nears completion, the Office of the United States Trade Representative has proposed imposing additional tariffs of 12.5 percent on India and 53 other countries. The proposal, issued under Section 301, alleges that these countries have failed to adequately prohibit forced labour in the production of exported goods.

India has rejected the allegations outright. Bloomberg reported that New Delhi has urged Washington to terminate the investigation. But the timing is awkward: the tariff proposal is under public consultation, with written submissions due by July 6 and hearings beginning July 7. A final decision is expected in June or July — potentially just as the interim trade deal is being signed.

The Commerce Ministry said on Wednesday that India "continues to engage with the United States" on the Section 301 proposals, suggesting that the tariff threat is being addressed alongside, rather than separately from, the bilateral trade agreement.

## What the Deal Covers

India's chief negotiator, Additional Secretary Darpan Jain, is leading the Indian side. The framework for the interim agreement was set by a joint statement issued on February 7, 2026, when both countries agreed to pursue a reciprocal and mutually beneficial trade pact while continuing negotiations on the broader BTA.

An Indian delegation visited Washington from April 20 to 23 for in-person meetings. The current round in New Delhi is the follow-up, and officials on both sides have described it as the most substantive yet.

The deal is expected to address tariff reductions on specific product categories, streamlined customs procedures and non-tariff barriers that have long frustrated American exporters. For India, the priority is securing relief from Section 301 measures and negotiating tariff rates lower than those imposed on competing economies.

Once the interim agreement is finalised, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer is expected to visit India for a formal signing.

## Why It Matters for the Diaspora

For Indian professionals and businesses in the US, the trade agreement has implications that go beyond tariff schedules. Economic security alignment, one of the negotiation pillars, could shape how the two countries coordinate on technology transfer, supply chain resilience and investment screening — areas that directly affect the Indian tech workforce and the thousands of companies that operate across both markets.

The deal also comes at a moment when the broader US-India economic relationship is under pressure from multiple directions. The Iran war has disrupted energy trade. The $100,000 H-1B premium processing fee, which more than 200,000 applicants paid in fiscal year 2026, has become a flashpoint. And the proposed elimination of "duration of status" for student visas has alarmed Indian graduates.

A completed trade agreement would be a counterweight — a signal that the economic relationship is deepening even as friction points multiply. The "99 percent" figure is politically useful for both sides. Whether the remaining one percent includes the Section 301 tariffs, or sits beside them as an unresolved irritant, will determine how the deal is received in both capitals and in the diaspora communities watching from Houston, the Bay Area and New Jersey.
author: Diaspora Desk
